props.title: Shoah
props.initialSlug: Epic Holocaust doc reveals survivors' untold stories

sections.content: **Shoah** (1985) stands as the definitive Holocaust documentary, a monumental 9.5-hour film that revolutionized how we confront historical atrocity through cinema. Director Claude Lanzmann rejected archival footage entirely, instead filming extensive interviews with survivors, witnesses, and even perpetrators. The film's power comes from its methodical approach - Lanzmann's patient, persistent questioning draws out devastating testimonies while his camera lingers on the peaceful present-day locations of former death camps, creating a chilling contrast. Unlike Night and Fog (1956), which relied heavily on graphic archival footage, Shoah forces viewers to imagine the horrors through firsthand accounts.

sections.content: Lanzmann's approach influenced a new wave of Holocaust documentaries that prioritized testimony and memory over historical footage. **The Last Days** (1998) focused on Hungarian Jews' experiences through five survivors' stories. **Into the Arms of Strangers: Stories of the Kindertransport** (2000) documented the British rescue of Jewish children. These films follow Shoah's lead in building their narratives around witness testimony while adding carefully selected archival materials that Lanzmann had rejected. SUBHEAD: Impact on Documentary Filmmaking

Beyond Holocaust cinema, Shoah transformed documentary approaches to historical trauma. **The Act of Killing** (2012) borrowed Lanzmann's technique of interviewing perpetrators, pushing them to confront their actions in the Indonesian genocide. **S21: The Khmer Rouge Killing Machine** (2003) similarly brought together survivors and guards from Cambodia's killing fields. Both films echo Shoah's unflinching examination of how ordinary people participate in mass murder. The film's influence extends to works like **The Look of Silence** (2014), which focuses on one family's confrontation with their brother's killers during the Indonesian purges.
